guide.what: An adverb (adverbio) tells you how, when, where, how much or how sure something is. It never changes its ending for gender or number: 'muy cansado', 'muy cansadas'.

rules.d: Adverbs go with a verb, an adjective, another adverb or a whole sentence. They do not change form (no -a or -s endings).
rules.ex: Ella maneja muy bien, pero hoy está bastante cansada.
rules.exEn: She drives very well, but today she's quite tired.

rules.d: Take the feminine form of the adjective and add -mente: lenta → lentamente. Adjectives with one form just add it: fácil → fácilmente. A written accent stays: rápida → rápidamente.

rules.t: Two -mente adverbs: only the last keeps -mente
rules.d: When you join two -mente adverbs with y, o or pero, the first one stays as the feminine adjective.
rules.exEn: She did it quickly and correctly.

rules.d: Muy goes before adjectives and adverbs (muy grande, muy tarde). Mucho goes with verbs (trabaja mucho) and before más, menos, mejor, peor, mayor, menor. Never say 'muy mucho'.
rules.ex: Estoy muy cansado porque trabajé mucho, mucho más que ayer.
rules.exEn: I'm very tired because I worked a lot, much more than yesterday.

rules.d: If nunca, nada, nadie, tampoco or jamás comes after the verb, you must also put no before the verb. If the negative word comes first, drop no.
rules.ex: No voy nunca al cine. / Nunca voy al cine.
rules.exEn: I never go to the movies.

rules.d: Quizás, quizá, tal vez and acaso usually take the subjunctive when they come before the verb, especially for the future or real doubt. A lo mejor always takes the indicative. Ojalá (an interjection used like an adverb) always takes the subjunctive.
rules.ex: Tal vez llueva mañana. / A lo mejor llueve mañana. / Ojalá no llueva.
rules.exEn: Maybe it'll rain tomorrow. / Hopefully it won't rain.

rules.d: Aquí (acá) = near me. Ahí = near you or not far. Allí (allá) = far from both of us. In Panama and Latin America acá and allá are very common in speech.
rules.ex: Mi celular está aquí, el tuyo está ahí y el carro está allá.
rules.exEn: My phone is here, yours is there, and the car is over there.

rules.d: Ya = already / now / (with no) not anymore. Todavía (or aún) = still, and with no = not yet. Answer '¿Ya comiste?' with 'Sí, ya' or 'No, todavía no'.
rules.ex: Ya no vivo en Colón, pero todavía trabajo allá.
rules.exEn: I don't live in Colón anymore, but I still work there.

rules.d: Adverbs usually go right after the verb or right before the adjective they change. Time and doubt adverbs can also open the sentence. Do not put an adverb between haber and the participle: 'he comido ya' or 'ya he comido', not 'he ya comido'.

mistakes.why: Use muy before adjectives; mucho goes with verbs.

mistakes.wrong: Nunca no voy a la playa. / Voy nunca a la playa.
mistakes.right: Nunca voy a la playa. / No voy nunca a la playa.
mistakes.why: Negative word before the verb: no 'no'. After the verb: add 'no' before it.
Build -mente on the feminine adjective and keep its accent.
With two -mente adverbs, only the last one keeps -mente.

mistakes.wrong: Actualmente, no me gusta el café. (meaning 'actually')
mistakes.right: En realidad, no me gusta el café.
mistakes.why: Actualmente means 'currently'; 'actually' is en realidad or realmente.

mistakes.wrong: Todavía no lo he terminado ya.
mistakes.why: Todavía no = not yet; don't add ya, which means 'already'.

items.use: Goes right before the verb (and before object pronouns): No lo sé. It is also the answer word 'no'.
items.ex: No quiero ir a la oficina hoy.
items.exEn: I don't want to go to the office today.

items.use: With an accent it means 'yes'; si without accent means 'if'. Also adds emphasis: Ella sí sabe.
items.ex: —¿Vienes mañana? —Sí, claro.
items.exEn: —Are you coming tomorrow? —Yes, of course.

items.use: Only before adjectives and adverbs: muy bueno, muy tarde. With verbs use mucho; never 'muy mucho'.
items.ex: El tráfico en Panamá está muy pesado hoy.
items.exEn: Traffic in Panama is very heavy today.

items.use: Comparisons: más ... que (more ... than). Superlative with el/la: el más caro. Always written with an accent; mas without accent is an old word for 'but'.
items.ex: Este celular es más caro que el otro.
items.exEn: This phone is more expensive than the other one.

items.use: Bien is the adverb (well); bueno is the adjective (good). Use 'estar bien' for 'to be fine'. Muy bien = very well.
items.ex: —¿Cómo estás? —Bien, gracias.
items.exEn: —How are you? —Fine, thanks.

items.use: Ya = already or right now; ya no = not anymore. Answer '¿Ya comiste?' with 'Sí, ya' or 'Todavía no'.
items.ex: Ya terminé el informe.
items.exEn: I already finished the report.
items.latam: In Panama '¡Ya!' or 'ya, ya' often means 'okay, got it' or 'enough'.

items.use: Means 'right here, near me'. Acá is the same idea and is very common in Latin American speech.
items.ex: Aquí se habla español.
items.exEn: Spanish is spoken here.

items.use: Use to agree with a positive statement: —Me gusta. —A mí también. For negatives use tampoco.
items.ex: Yo también vivo en Ciudad de Panamá.
items.exEn: I live in Panama City too.

items.use: Accent in questions and exclamations: ¿Cómo estás? ¡Cómo llueve! Como without accent means 'like/as' or 'since'.
items.ex: ¿Cómo se dice 'computer' en español?
items.exEn: How do you say 'computer' in Spanish?

items.use: As an adverb it goes with verbs and does not change: trabajan mucho. Also before más, menos, mejor, peor: mucho mejor.
items.ex: Mi hermano trabaja mucho.
items.exEn: My brother works a lot.

items.en: like this; like that; this way
items.use: Así se hace = this is how it's done. Así que = so (result). Así así = so-so.
items.ex: No lo hagas así; hazlo así.
items.exEn: Don't do it like that; do it like this.

items.use: Ahora mismo = right now. Hasta ahora = until now / see you soon.
items.ex: Ahora vivo en Panamá.
items.exEn: Now I live in Panama.

items.use: As an adverb it means 'only' and is written without an accent (the old 'sólo' is no longer needed). Same as solamente.
items.ex: Solo quiero un café, por favor.
items.exEn: I just want a coffee, please.

items.use: Accent in questions: ¿Dónde vives? Use adónde for movement 'to where'. Donde without accent links clauses: la casa donde vivo.
items.ex: ¿Dónde está el baño?
items.exEn: Where is the bathroom?

items.use: Shortened tanto, used before adjectives and adverbs: tan alto. Comparisons of equality: tan ... como (as ... as).
items.ex: Mi carro no es tan nuevo como el tuyo.
items.exEn: My car isn't as new as yours.

items.use: Before the verb alone (Nunca bebo café) or after it with no (No bebo nunca café). Both are correct.
items.ex: Nunca llego tarde al trabajo.
items.exEn: I'm never late for work.

items.use: Usually right after the verb or at the start: Siempre como aquí. Como siempre = as always.
items.ex: Siempre desayuno a las siete.
items.exEn: I always have breakfast at seven.

items.use: In time: back then / next. In speech it often means 'so' (a result). Desde entonces = since then.
items.ex: Entonces vivíamos en David.
items.exEn: Back then we lived in David.

items.use: Middle distance: near the listener or not far. Don't confuse with hay (there is) or ay (ouch).
items.ex: Pon la caja ahí, al lado de la puerta.
items.exEn: Put the box there, next to the door.
items.latam: Very common in Panama: 'Ahí vamos' (getting by) and 'Ahí nos vemos' (see you around).

items.use: Accent in questions: ¿Cuándo llegas? Cuando without accent links clauses and takes subjunctive for the future: cuando llegues.
items.ex: ¿Cuándo empieza la clase?
items.exEn: When does the class start?

items.use: Poco = not much (negative feeling); un poco = a little (neutral). Habla poco vs habla un poco.
items.ex: Duermo poco cuando tengo exámenes.
items.exEn: I don't sleep much when I have exams.

items.use: Antes de + infinitive or noun: antes de comer. Antes que nada = first of all.
items.ex: Lávate las manos antes de comer.
items.exEn: Wash your hands before eating.

items.use: Después de + infinitive or noun: después del trabajo. Alone it means 'later'.
items.ex: Te llamo después del trabajo.
items.exEn: I'll call you after work.

items.use: Comparisons: menos ... que. Also 'minus' and telling time: las dos menos diez.
items.ex: Ahora gasto menos dinero en gasolina.
items.exEn: Now I spend less money on gas.

items.use: Hoy en día = nowadays. Hoy por la mañana = this morning.
items.ex: Hoy tengo una reunión a las tres.
items.exEn: Today I have a meeting at three.

items.use: As an adverb it means 'tomorrow'; la mañana (noun) is 'the morning'. Mañana por la mañana = tomorrow morning.
items.ex: Mañana voy al banco.
items.exEn: Tomorrow I'm going to the bank.

items.use: Like allí but less exact and often with movement: Ven para acá; ve para allá. Más allá = further.
items.ex: Mis papás viven allá en Chiriquí.
items.exEn: My parents live over there in Chiriquí.
items.latam: Much more used than allí in Panama and Latin America. In Spain allí is more common.

items.use: Same meaning as aquí, a bit less exact and common with movement: ven acá, para acá.
items.ex: Ven acá un momento, por favor.
items.exEn: Come here a moment, please.
items.latam: Very common in Panama and Latin America; in Spain people prefer aquí.

items.use: The far point: away from both speaker and listener. In speech, many Latin Americans say allá instead.
items.ex: ¿Ves ese edificio? Allí trabaja mi esposa.
items.exEn: See that building? My wife works there.

items.use: Todavía = still; todavía no = not yet. Same meaning as aún with an accent.
items.ex: Todavía no he terminado la tarea.
items.exEn: I haven't finished the homework yet.

items.use: Then / afterwards: primero ..., luego ... Hasta luego = see you later.
items.ex: Primero vamos al súper y luego a la casa.
items.exEn: First we go to the supermarket and then home.

items.use: As an adverb it goes with verbs: No trabajes tanto. Comparisons: tanto como (as much as). Before adjectives it becomes tan.
items.ex: No comas tanto, que después te duele la barriga.
items.exEn: Don't eat so much, your stomach will hurt later.

items.use: Mal is the adverb (badly); malo is the adjective (bad). Estar mal = to be unwell or wrong.
items.ex: Dormí mal anoche por el calor.
items.exEn: I slept badly last night because of the heat.

items.use: Usually with the preterite: Ayer fui. Ayer por la tarde = yesterday afternoon.
items.ex: Ayer llovió toda la tarde.
items.exEn: Yesterday it rained all afternoon.

items.use: Llegar tarde = to be late. La tarde (noun) is 'the afternoon'. Más vale tarde que nunca.
items.ex: Siempre llega tarde a las reuniones.
items.exEn: He always arrives late to meetings.

items.use: Opposite of tarde. Más temprano = earlier.
items.ex: Mañana me levanto temprano para ir al aeropuerto.
items.exEn: Tomorrow I'm getting up early to go to the airport.

items.use: Goes before what it changes: casi siempre, casi nunca, casi todos. With the present for past events: Casi me caigo.
items.ex: Casi pierdo el bus esta mañana.
items.exEn: I almost missed the bus this morning.

items.use: The negative of también: —No me gusta. —A mí tampoco. After the verb it needs no: No voy tampoco.
items.ex: Yo tampoco entiendo la tarea.
items.exEn: I don't understand the homework either.

items.use: With an accent it means 'still/yet', the same as todavía: aún no = not yet. Without accent (aun) it means 'even'.
items.ex: Aún no sé si puedo ir.
items.exEn: I still don't know if I can go.

items.use: The everyday way to say 'sometimes'. It goes at the start or end of the sentence. Algunas veces is also correct but less common.
items.ex: A veces trabajo desde la casa.
items.exEn: Sometimes I work from home.

items.use: Can mean 'approximately' or 'so-so' as an answer to ¿Cómo estás?
items.ex: —¿Qué tal el examen? —Más o menos.
items.exEn: —How was the exam? —So-so.

items.use: Quizá and quizás are both correct. Before the verb it usually takes the subjunctive: Quizás venga. With the indicative you sound more sure.
items.ex: Quizás vaya a la playa este fin de semana.
items.exEn: Maybe I'll go to the beach this weekend.
items.latam: Quizás is more common in Latin America; quizá is a bit more common in Spain.

items.use: Same as quizás: usually subjunctive after it when it comes first: Tal vez llueva. Write it as two words.
items.ex: Tal vez llegue un poco tarde.
items.exEn: Maybe I'll arrive a bit late.

items.use: Before adjectives = too: demasiado caro. With verbs = too much: comes demasiado. As an adverb it does not change.
items.ex: Este apartamento es demasiado caro para mí.
items.exEn: This apartment is too expensive for me.
items.latam: In Panama and parts of Latin America, demasiado can also mean just 'really, very' in a positive way: 'Está demasiado bueno.'

items.use: Before adjectives = quite/fairly: bastante bien. After verbs = a fair amount: Estudió bastante.
items.ex: El examen fue bastante difícil.
items.exEn: The exam was quite difficult.

items.use: Hasta pronto = see you soon. De pronto = suddenly. Lo más pronto posible = as soon as possible.
items.ex: Pronto voy a cambiar de trabajo.
items.exEn: I'm going to change jobs soon.
items.latam: In Spain pronto also means 'early' (temprano); in Latin America it mostly means 'soon'.

items.use: Cerca de + place: cerca de la oficina. Opposite: lejos.
items.ex: Vivo cerca del metro.
items.exEn: I live near the metro.

items.use: Lejos de + place. Opposite of cerca.
items.ex: El aeropuerto queda lejos de mi casa.
items.exEn: The airport is far from my house.
items.latam: 'Quedar' (to be located) is very common in Panama: ¿Dónde queda?

items.use: Dentro de + noun: dentro de la caja. Also time: dentro de dos días = in two days.
items.ex: Las llaves están dentro de la mochila.
items.exEn: The keys are inside the backpack.

items.use: Fuera de + noun: fuera de la ciudad. Estar fuera = to be away.
items.ex: Esta semana estoy fuera del país.
items.exEn: This week I'm out of the country.

items.use: Used alone, often with movement: Vamos adentro. With de, dentro is preferred: dentro de la casa.
items.ex: Hace mucho calor; vamos adentro.
items.exEn: It's very hot; let's go inside.
items.latam: Adentro and afuera are much more used in Latin America; Spain prefers dentro and fuera.

items.use: Used alone, often with movement: Salgan afuera. With de use fuera: fuera de la casa.
items.ex: Los niños están jugando afuera.
items.exEn: The kids are playing outside.
items.latam: Very common in Panama; Spain prefers fuera.

items.use: Used alone: Vive arriba. For 'on top of' something use encima de. ¡Arriba! = come on!
items.ex: Mi oficina está arriba, en el tercer piso.
items.exEn: My office is upstairs, on the third floor.

items.use: Used alone: Te espero abajo. For 'under' something use debajo de.
items.ex: Te espero abajo, en la entrada.
items.exEn: I'll wait for you downstairs, at the entrance.

items.use: Also written en seguida (both correct). Very common with waiters and shop staff.
items.ex: Enseguida le traigo la cuenta.
items.exEn: I'll bring you the check right away.
items.latam: In Panama you may also hear 'de una' (right away) in casual speech.

items.use: Same as otra vez and volver a + infinitive. Goes after the verb or at the end.
items.ex: Se fue la luz de nuevo.
items.exEn: The power went out again.

items.use: Very common in speech. Never 'una otra vez'.
items.ex: ¿Puedes repetirlo otra vez, por favor?
items.exEn: Can you repeat it again, please?

items.use: A bit more formal than muchas veces or seguido. Goes after the verb or at the end.
items.ex: Viajo a menudo por trabajo.
items.exEn: I travel often for work.
items.latam: In everyday Latin American speech 'seguido' is also used: Voy seguido a la playa.

items.use: Shows relief after waiting. Different from finalmente (lastly, in a list).
items.ex: ¡Por fin llegó el fin de semana!
items.exEn: The weekend is finally here!

items.use: Usually with the preterite to tell a story. Same as de pronto.
items.ex: Estábamos en la playa y de repente empezó a llover.
items.exEn: We were at the beach and suddenly it started to rain.
items.latam: In some Latin American countries de repente can also mean 'maybe'.

items.use: Same as de repente.
items.ex: De pronto se fue la luz.
items.exEn: Suddenly the power went out.

items.use: Very common in speech. Unlike quizás and tal vez, it always takes the indicative: A lo mejor viene.
items.ex: A lo mejor vamos al cine esta noche.
items.exEn: Maybe we'll go to the movies tonight.

items.use: As a question it means 'Really?': ¿De verdad? It also stresses that something is true.
items.ex: De verdad, no sabía nada.
items.exEn: Really, I didn't know anything.

items.use: ¿En serio? = Really? Tomar en serio = to take seriously.
items.ex: ¿En serio te vas a mudar a Boquete?
items.exEn: Are you seriously moving to Boquete?

items.use: A strong 'yes'. Por supuesto que sí / que no.
items.ex: —¿Me ayudas? —Por supuesto.
items.exEn: —Will you help me? —Of course.

items.en: right now; in a little while
items.use: Diminutive of ahora. Its meaning depends on tone and context: it can mean 'this very second' or 'later, in a bit'.
items.ex: Ahorita te llamo, estoy manejando.
items.exEn: I'll call you in a bit, I'm driving.
items.latam: Very common in Panama, Mexico and the Caribbean. In Panama 'ahorita' often means 'soon, not right now'. Not used much in Spain.

items.use: Stronger than ahora. In Spain it can also mean 'in a minute'.
items.ex: Ahora mismo no puedo hablar.
items.exEn: I can't talk right now.

items.use: As an answer it means 'of course'. Claro que sí / claro que no. Hablar claro = to speak clearly.
items.ex: —¿Puedo pasar? —Claro, adelante.
items.exEn: —Can I come in? —Sure, go ahead.

items.use: Means 'really, truly'. For 'actually' (in fact) you can also say en realidad.
items.ex: Realmente me gusta vivir aquí.
items.exEn: I really like living here.

items.use: The correct way to say 'actually'. Not actualmente.
items.ex: En realidad, no me gusta el café.
items.exEn: Actually, I don't like coffee.

items.use: More common than afortunadamente in speech.
items.ex: Por suerte, encontré mis llaves.
items.exEn: Luckily, I found my keys.

items.use: Adds a surprising extra: Incluso mi abuela usa WhatsApp. Same as hasta in speech.
items.ex: Trabaja todos los días, incluso los domingos.
items.exEn: He works every day, even on Sundays.

items.use: Adds information. Además de + noun or infinitive: además de trabajar, estudia.
items.ex: Además de inglés, habla francés.
items.exEn: Besides English, she speaks French.

items.use: Asks about destination with movement verbs: ¿Adónde vas? You can also say ¿A dónde vas? Without accent (adonde) it links clauses.
items.ex: ¿Adónde vamos a comer hoy?
items.exEn: Where are we going to eat today?

items.use: Used alone, often with movement: Vamos atrás. Años atrás = years ago. For 'behind something' use detrás de.
items.ex: Siéntate atrás, que adelante va mi mamá.
items.exEn: Sit in the back; my mom is riding in front.
items.latam: In Latin America atrás de is also used for detrás de.

items.use: Used alone, often with movement. ¡Adelante! = come in / go ahead. En adelante = from now on.
items.ex: Sigue adelante dos cuadras.
items.exEn: Keep going straight for two blocks.
items.latam: In Latin America adelante de is also used for delante de.

items.use: Delante de + noun = in front of. More static than adelante.
items.ex: Hay un carro estacionado delante de mi casa.
items.exEn: There's a car parked in front of my house.

items.use: Detrás de + noun = behind. More static than atrás.
items.ex: El supermercado está detrás del banco.
items.exEn: The supermarket is behind the bank.

items.use: Encima de + noun = on top of. Por encima = above, over. Encima also means 'on top of that, what's more'.
items.ex: Deja el celular encima de la mesa.
items.exEn: Leave the phone on the table.

items.use: Debajo de + noun = under. Not the same as abajo (downstairs, below in general).
items.ex: El gato está debajo de la cama.
items.exEn: The cat is under the bed.

items.use: Alrededor de + noun = around. Also 'about, approximately': alrededor de cien personas.
items.ex: Caminamos alrededor del lago.
items.exEn: We walked around the lake.

items.use: Enfrente de + noun = across from, facing. Can also be written en frente.
items.ex: La farmacia está enfrente del hospital.
items.exEn: The pharmacy is across from the hospital.

items.use: One word. Usually with the preterite.
items.ex: Anoche vimos una película en casa.
items.exEn: Last night we watched a movie at home.

items.use: Stronger than nunca. Same rules: before the verb alone, or after it with no. Nunca jamás = never ever.
items.ex: Jamás he visto tanta lluvia.
items.exEn: I have never seen so much rain.

items.use: Barely: Apenas dormí. Also 'as soon as' (+ subjunctive for the future): Apenas llegues, llámame.
items.ex: Apenas tengo tiempo para almorzar.
items.exEn: I barely have time for lunch.

items.use: Common request: Más despacio, por favor. Same as lentamente but more everyday.
items.ex: ¿Puede hablar más despacio, por favor?
items.exEn: Can you speak more slowly, please?

items.use: Very common for slow progress.
items.ex: Poco a poco estoy mejorando mi español.
items.exEn: Little by little I'm improving my Spanish.

items.use: As an adverb it does not change: Ellas corren rápido. Very common instead of rápidamente.
items.ex: No manejes tan rápido.
items.exEn: Don't drive so fast.
items.latam: In Latin America rápido is the everyday word; Spain also uses deprisa.

items.use: Also used alone as 'Exactly!' to agree.
items.ex: Eso es exactamente lo que necesito.
items.exEn: That's exactly what I need.

items.use: Usually takes the indicative; the subjunctive is possible when it comes first and you're less sure.
items.ex: Probablemente llego a las ocho.
items.exEn: I'll probably arrive at eight.

items.use: Often means 'just': Simplemente no quiero.
items.ex: Simplemente no tengo tiempo.
items.exEn: I just don't have time.

items.use: Often at the start of the sentence. Same as generalmente.
items.ex: Normalmente almuerzo en la oficina.
items.exEn: I usually have lunch at the office.

items.use: Same as solo, a bit more emphatic. No solamente ... sino también = not only ... but also.
items.ex: Solamente tengo cinco dólares.
items.exEn: I only have five dollars.

items.use: Before participles it means 'newly': recién casados, recién llegado. In much of Latin America it also goes before verbs: Recién llegué.
items.ex: Recién llegué de la oficina.
items.exEn: I just got back from the office.
items.latam: Spain uses recién only before participles (recién hecho) and says 'acabo de llegar' instead.

items.use: The strong form of mucho with verbs: Te quiero muchísimo. Don't use it before adjectives (use muy or -ísimo on the adjective).
items.ex: Me gustó muchísimo el concierto.
items.exEn: I loved the concert.

items.use: Strong agreement: Totalmente de acuerdo.
items.ex: Estoy totalmente de acuerdo contigo.
items.exEn: I totally agree with you.

items.use: Close to totalmente. Common with adjectives: completamente lleno.
items.ex: El restaurante estaba completamente lleno.
items.exEn: The restaurant was completely full.

items.use: Used to end a list or a story. For relief after waiting, por fin is more natural.
items.ex: Finalmente decidimos quedarnos en casa.
items.exEn: In the end we decided to stay home.

items.use: Highlights one item: Me gusta la fruta, especialmente el mango.
items.ex: Hace calor, especialmente en abril.
items.exEn: It's hot, especially in April.

items.use: Same as especialmente. Two words.
items.ex: Me encanta la comida panameña, sobre todo el sancocho.
items.exEn: I love Panamanian food, especially sancocho.

items.use: Same as al menos. Goes before what it limits.
items.ex: Llámame por lo menos una vez a la semana.
items.exEn: Call me at least once a week.

items.use: Careful: it usually means 'probably', not 'certainly'. Normally takes the indicative.
items.ex: Seguramente está atrapado en el tráfico.
items.exEn: He's probably stuck in traffic.

items.use: Common at the start of the sentence.
items.ex: Obviamente, no voy a salir con esta lluvia.
items.exEn: Obviously, I'm not going out in this rain.

items.use: Formed from clara + -mente.
items.ex: El profesor explicó todo claramente.
items.exEn: The teacher explained everything clearly.

items.use: Keeps the accent from rápida. In speech, rápido is more common.
items.ex: El agua subió rápidamente.
items.exEn: The water rose quickly.

items.use: From lenta + -mente. Despacio is more common in speech.
items.ex: El tráfico avanzaba lentamente.
items.exEn: Traffic was moving slowly.

items.use: Keeps the accent from fácil. Fácil also works as an adverb in speech: Se hace fácil.
items.ex: Puedes llegar fácilmente en metro.
items.exEn: You can get there easily by metro.

items.use: Usually with the present or present perfect: Últimamente he dormido mal.
items.ex: Últimamente llueve todas las tardes.
items.exEn: Lately it rains every afternoon.

items.use: False friend: it means 'currently', not 'actually'. 'Actually' = en realidad.
items.ex: Actualmente trabajo en un banco.
items.exEn: I currently work at a bank.

items.use: Common in essays for the DELE writing task.
items.ex: Hoy en día todo el mundo tiene celular.
items.exEn: Nowadays everyone has a cell phone.

items.use: Less often than a veces. Goes at the start or end.
items.ex: De vez en cuando como comida china.
items.exEn: I eat Chinese food from time to time.

items.use: Llegar a tiempo = to arrive on time. En punto = on the dot.
items.ex: Por suerte, llegamos a tiempo al vuelo.
items.exEn: Luckily, we made it to the flight on time.

items.use: Usually with the preterite.
items.ex: Anteayer fui al médico.
items.exEn: The day before yesterday I went to the doctor.
items.latam: In Panama and most of Latin America people usually say 'antier'.

items.use: Mostly in questions that show surprise or doubt: ¿Acaso no lo sabías? Por si acaso = just in case.
items.ex: ¿Acaso crees que no me di cuenta?
items.exEn: Do you really think I didn't notice?

items.use: An interjection used like an adverb. Always takes the subjunctive: Ojalá (que) llueva. Past subjunctive = unlikely wish: Ojalá tuviera tiempo.
items.ex: Ojalá que no haya tráfico.
items.exEn: Hopefully there's no traffic.

items.use: Means 'definitely'. Also 'for good': Se fue definitivamente.
items.ex: Definitivamente, este es el mejor ceviche de la ciudad.
items.exEn: This is definitely the best ceviche in the city.

items.use: Strong agreement. Sin duda alguna is even stronger.
items.ex: Sin duda, es la mejor época para visitar.
items.exEn: Without a doubt, it's the best time to visit.

items.use: More formal than enseguida.
items.ex: Llame inmediatamente si hay una emergencia.
items.exEn: Call immediately if there is an emergency.

items.use: Strong: absolutamente nada = absolutely nothing.
items.ex: No entendí absolutamente nada.
items.exEn: I understood absolutely nothing.

items.use: Often 'straight to': Ve directamente a la casa.
items.ex: Después del trabajo me fui directamente a la casa.
items.exEn: After work I went straight home.

items.use: Stresses the exact thing: Precisamente por eso = that's exactly why.
items.ex: Precisamente de eso quería hablarte.
items.exEn: That's exactly what I wanted to talk to you about.

items.use: Very common with entender: Te entiendo perfectamente.
items.ex: Te entiendo perfectamente.
items.exEn: I understand you perfectly.

items.use: Means 'almost, nearly', like casi.
items.ex: Prácticamente todos llegaron tarde.
items.exEn: Practically everyone arrived late.

items.use: Shows what seems true. Same as al parecer.
items.ex: Aparentemente, cancelaron el vuelo.
items.exEn: Apparently, they canceled the flight.

items.use: Very common reply: —¡Buen fin de semana! —¡Igualmente!
items.ex: —Mucho gusto. —Igualmente.
items.exEn: —Nice to meet you. —Likewise.

items.use: Also written de prisa. Same as rápido.
items.ex: Comí deprisa porque se me hacía tarde.
items.exEn: I ate quickly because I was running late.
items.latam: Used more in Spain; in Panama people say rápido or 'apúrate' (hurry up).

items.use: More formal than recién or hace poco.
items.ex: Recientemente abrieron un restaurante nuevo.
items.exEn: They recently opened a new restaurant.

items.use: More formal than otra vez or de nuevo; common in news.
items.ex: El presidente habló nuevamente sobre el canal.
items.exEn: The president spoke again about the canal.

items.use: Introduces your opinion: Personalmente, prefiero ... Also 'in person'.
items.ex: Personalmente, prefiero la playa.
items.exEn: Personally, I prefer the beach.

items.use: Common in speech to sum up.
items.ex: Básicamente, no hay suficiente dinero.
items.exEn: Basically, there isn't enough money.

items.use: Can mean 'of course' or 'in a natural way'.
items.ex: Naturalmente, te voy a ayudar.
items.exEn: Naturally, I'll help you.

items.use: Goes before numbers. Same as más o menos or alrededor de.
items.ex: El viaje dura aproximadamente dos horas.
items.exEn: The trip takes approximately two hours.

items.use: Before the verb, often with the subjunctive: Posiblemente llegue tarde.
items.ex: Posiblemente cambien el horario.
items.exEn: They'll possibly change the schedule.

items.use: Same as normalmente. Por lo general is a common alternative.
items.ex: Generalmente salgo del trabajo a las cinco.
items.exEn: I usually leave work at five.

items.use: Points to the main reason or part.
items.ex: Vine a Panamá principalmente por trabajo.
items.exEn: I came to Panama mainly for work.

items.use: Introduces an honest opinion. Also 'Sincerely' at the end of a formal letter.
items.ex: Sinceramente, no me gustó la película.
items.exEn: Honestly, I didn't like the movie.

items.use: Same as lamentablemente and por desgracia.
items.ex: Desafortunadamente, la tienda ya cerró.
items.exEn: Unfortunately, the store already closed.

items.use: Same as por suerte, which is more common in speech.
items.ex: Afortunadamente, nadie salió herido.
items.exEn: Fortunately, nobody got hurt.

items.use: Shows doubt about what others say.
items.ex: Supuestamente, el bus pasa cada diez minutos.
items.exEn: Supposedly, the bus comes every ten minutes.

items.use: More formal than a menudo or seguido.
items.ex: Frecuentemente hay tranques en la Transístmica.
items.exEn: There are frequently traffic jams on the Transístmica.
items.latam: 'Tranque' is the Panamanian word for traffic jam.

items.use: Informal. Means 'just/only' or softens a request: Pase nomás (go ahead and come in).
items.ex: Pase nomás, la puerta está abierta.
items.exEn: Just come in, the door is open.
items.latam: Typical of Mexico and the Andes; less common in Panama and rare in Spain (no más).

items.use: As an adverb it does not change: Ella está medio cansada (not 'media').
items.ex: Estoy medio cansado hoy.
items.exEn: I'm kind of tired today.
items.latam: Very common in Latin American speech.

items.use: Before the verb alone; after it, add no: No me saludó ni siquiera.
items.ex: Ni siquiera me dijo adiós.
items.exEn: He didn't even say goodbye to me.

items.use: Without an accent it means 'even' (= incluso, hasta). With accent (aún) it means 'still'. Aun así = even so.
items.ex: Estaba cansado, pero aun así fue a trabajar.
items.exEn: He was tired, but even so he went to work.

items.use: Lo hizo a propósito = he did it on purpose. At the start of a sentence it also means 'by the way'.
items.ex: No lo hice a propósito, perdón.
items.exEn: I didn't do it on purpose, sorry.

items.use: Also 'inside out' or 'upside down' for clothes or objects.
items.ex: Tienes la camiseta al revés.
items.exEn: Your T-shirt is inside out.

items.use: Goes before adjectives; stronger than muy.
items.ex: Cuidado, el café está extremadamente caliente.
items.exEn: Careful, the coffee is extremely hot.

items.use: Note the order in Spanish: late or early.
items.ex: Tarde o temprano vas a tener que decidir.
items.exEn: Sooner or later you'll have to decide.

items.use: Same as desafortunadamente; very common in speech.
items.ex: Por desgracia, no quedan boletos.
items.exEn: Unfortunately, there are no tickets left.

items.use: Con cuidado is more common in speech.
items.ex: Lee el contrato cuidadosamente antes de firmar.
items.exEn: Read the contract carefully before signing.
